parole.significato: Forms an alternative plural ending for words borrowed from Italian that end in ⟨o⟩ or ⟨e⟩ in the singular.
parole.testo: From Italian -i (masculine plural), from Latin -ī (see etymology 2).

parole.significato: Used to form feminine nouns.
parole.testo: From Italian -ina and its etymon Classical Latin -īna. In some instances perhaps also partly via Spanish -ina. Doublet of -ine.

parole.significato: The fermionic supersymmetric partner of a boson (a bosino), symbolized by a tilde over the nonsupersymmetric particle s…
parole.testo: From Italian -ino (“-ine, -o: forming diminutives”), from the dative form of Latin -īnus. In its use in physics, originally after the model of earlier neutrino, coined by Enrico Fermi in 1933. Internet slang usages gained currency in the second half of the 2010s.

parole.significato: An Italian abbot or other member of the clergy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian abate (“abbot”), from Latin abbātem, the accusative singular of abbās (“abbot”), from Ancient Greek ἀββᾶς (abbâs), a variant of ἀββᾱ (abbā, “father; title of respect for an abbot”), from Aramaic אַבָּא (’abbā, “father; ancestor; teacher; chief, leader; author, originator”), fro

parole.significato: A layer of tissue that separates the iliac artery from the iliac fascia.
parole.testo: Named after John Abernethy, English surgeon, + fascia, which through Italian derives from Latin fascia.

parole.significato: A tempo mark directing that a passage is to be played at an increasing speed.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian accelerando, from Latin accelero.

parole.significato: To gratify, cause pleasure to.
parole.testo: From Italian aggradare /aggratare, from Latin aggrātāre.

parole.significato: A sweet-bitter liqueur originating from Italy (but also produced in Turkey), flavored with almonds and a secret blend-s…
parole.testo: From Italian amaretto, from amaro (“bitter”) (from Latin amarus) + diminutive suffix -etto.

parole.significato: affectionate; loving.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian amorevole + -ous, from Latin amor (“love”).

parole.significato: A breed of poultry.
parole.testo: From Italian Ancona, from Latin Ancōna, from ancōn (“curve, elbow”).

parole.significato: To perform antics, to caper.
parole.testo: Probably from Italian antico (“ancient”), used to describe ancient wall paintings from classical times, from Latin antiquus (“venerable”). See also Italian grottesco (“grotesque”). Doublet of antique.

parole.significato: A northern Italian variety of short-grained starchy rice with a white dot at the center of each grain, commonly used in…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian arborio, from Arborio, a town in Piedmont; the toponym is most likely linked to Latin arboreus (“wooden, tree-like”). Compare English arboreous.

parole.significato: Preceded by the, and often in the form Archipelago: the Aegean Sea.
parole.testo: The noun is borrowed from Italian arcipelago (“Aegean Sea; group of many islands”), from arci- (variant of archi- (prefix meaning ‘foremost, primary’)) + pelago (“(open) sea”): * Archi- is derived from Latin archi-, from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓ρχῐ- (ărkhĭ-, prefix denoting primary authority or importance),

parole.significato: A musical piece written typically for a solo voice with orchestral accompaniment in an opera or cantata.
parole.testo: From Italian aria, metathesis from Latin āerem, accusative of āēr, from Ancient Greek ἀήρ (aḗr, “air”). Doublet of air.

parole.significato: A musical instrument made of blown-glass bowls mounted on a spindle turned originally by a foot pedal, and played with…
parole.testo: Coined by Benjamin Franklin, its inventor; built on Italian armonia (“harmony”). Glass harmonica is a corruption of Franklin's original word, a back-formation influenced by harmonica (a reed instrument invented sixty years later).

parole.significato: To fill up with alluvial earth.
parole.testo: From Italian atterrare. Compare Late Latin atterrare (“to cast to earth”).

parole.significato: The chrysalis of an insect, especially of a butterfly.
parole.testo: From Italian aurelia (“chrysalis”), from Latin aureus (“golden”).

parole.significato: In the form of four unhusked filberts.
parole.testo: From Italian avellana (“filbert”), from Latin Avella or Abella, a city of Campania.

parole.significato: A brothel.
parole.testo: From Italian bagno, from Latin balneum (“bath”). Doublet of bain, balaneion, and banya.

parole.significato: An accessible structure extending from a building, especially outside a window.
parole.testo: From Italian balcone (“balcony, floor-length window”), from Old Italian balcone (“scaffold”) from Lombardic *balk, *balko (“beam”), from Proto-Germanic *balkô (“beam”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰelǵ- (“beam, pile, prop”). Akin to Old High German balco, balcho (“beam”), Old English balca (“beam, ri

parole.significato: One who robs others in a lawless area, especially as part of a group.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian bandito (“outlawed”), a derivative of Italian bandire (“to ban”), from Late Latin bandīre, an alteration (due to Gothic 𐌱𐌰𐌽𐌳𐍅𐌾𐌰𐌽 (bandwjan, “to signal”)) of Late Latin bannīre (“to ban”), from Frankish *bannan (“to ban”). Doublet of bandito.

parole.significato: A type of needlepoint embroidery, traditionally in wool on canvas, consisting of upright flat stitches laid in a mathem…
parole.testo: After a series of chairs found in the Bargello palace in Florence, which have a similar pattern. The palace takes its name from Italian bargello (“police headquarters”), from Late Latin barigildus, derived from the Frankish or Gothic equivalent of English borough.

parole.significato: A bass singer, especially in opera.
parole.testo: From Italian basso, from Latin bassus (“short, low”). Doublet of base and bass.

parole.significato: A plant, Atropa belladonna, having purple bell-shaped flowers and poisonous black glossy berries.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian belladonna (altered by folk etymology: bella donna (“beautiful lady”)) from Medieval Latin blādōna (“nightshade”), of Gaulish origin. The folk etymology was motivated by the cosmetic use of nightshade for dilating the eyes.

parole.significato: The flat symbol (♭), or a flattened note.
parole.testo: From Italian bemolle, from Medieval Latin b molle (“B-flat”, literally “soft B”).

parole.significato: A sport, similar to bocce, designed to be played by people with impaired motor skills.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian boccia (“ball”), from Vulgar Latin *buttia, borrowed from Byzantine Greek βούττια (boúttia, plural of βούττιον (boúttion)), from Ancient Greek βοῦττις (boûttis), possibly borrowed from Pre-Greek. Doublet of butt (“wooden cask”).

parole.significato: A workshop or studio in Italy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian bottega.

parole.significato: A plant, Brassica oleracea var. italica, of the cabbage family, Brassicaceae; especially, the tree-shaped flower and st…
parole.testo: First attested in 1699, Italian broccoli, plural of broccolo (“cabbage sprout, head”), diminutive of brocco (“shoot, sprout”) (which is also the origin of brocade), from Latin broccus (“pointed, sharp, projecting; buck-toothed”), possibly of Gaulish origin, related to Proto-Celtic *brokkos (“badger”

parole.significato: A bust.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian busto.

parole.significato: A part of a piece of music, such as a concerto, that is very decorative and is played by a single musician.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian cadenza, from Latin cadentia. Doublet of cadence and chance.

parole.significato: Squid as food, especially cooked in the form of calamari rings.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian calamari, plural of calamaro, from Latin calamarius, from calamus, from Ancient Greek κάλαμος (kálamos, “reed, ink pen”).

parole.significato: A piece of jewelry, etc., carved in relief.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian cammeo, from Medieval Latin camaeus, of unknown origin. The movie sense is short for “cameo role” referring to a famous person who was playing no character, but him or herself. Like a cameo brooch — a low-relief carving of a person’s head or bust — the actor or celebrity is ins

parole.significato: A flat stretch of countryside; open rural plain.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian campagna, from Late Latin campānia. Doublet of champagne, campaign, and campania.

parole.significato: Open country.
parole.testo: From Italian campagna, respelled after its etymon Late Latin campānia (“open country, battlefield”) (compare the region Campania), from Latin campus (“field”). Doublet of campaign, campagna, and champagne.

parole.significato: A dog of an Italian breed valued as a companion, guardian and hunter.
parole.testo: From Italian cane corso (literally “Corsican dog”), with adjective corso being more likely derived from Latin cohors (“farmyard; enclosure”).

parole.significato: Wide tubes of pasta filled with a savoury stuffing and baked in the oven.
parole.testo: From Italian cannelloni, from Latin canna (“reed”).

parole.significato: A tempo mark directing that a passage is to be played in a lyrical manner
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian cantabile (“singable, capable being sung”), derived from cantare (“to sing”). See also Latin cantabilis (“worthy to be sung”).

parole.significato: A vocal melody or instrumental passage in a smooth, lyrical style.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian or Latin cantilēna.

parole.significato: A song.
parole.testo: From Italian canzone, from Latin cantiō, cantiōnem. Doublet of cantion, canzone, and chanson.

parole.significato: An Italian or Provençal song or ballad.
parole.testo: From Italian canzone (“song”), from Latin cantiō. Doublet of cantion and chanson.

parole.significato: A short song, now especially one which is light and breezy.
parole.testo: From Italian canzonetta, from canzone (“song”) + -etta (“-ette: forming diminutives”), from Latin cantiō. Doublet of canzonetta. Cf. canzone.

parole.significato: A style of popular Italian secular vocal composition which originated around 1560, or a piece composed in this style
parole.testo: From Italian canzonetta, from canzone (“song”) + -etta (“-ette: forming diminutives”), from Latin cantiō. Doublet of canzonet. Cf. canzone.

parole.significato: A leader in the Mafia; a caporegime.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian capo (“head, chief”). Doublet of cape, caput, chef, chief, head, and Howth.

parole.significato: A public building or room for gambling.
parole.testo: From Italian casino, diminutive form of casa (“house”), from Latin casa (“cottage, hut”).

parole.significato: A male who has been castrated, especially a male whose testicles have been removed before puberty in order to retain hi…
parole.testo: From Italian castrato, from Latin castrō (“to castrate”), likely from caedō (“to cut”).

parole.significato: Synonym of catafalque.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian catafalco.

parole.significato: A concave moulding with a regular curved profile that is part of a circle.
parole.testo: From Italian cavetto, from cavo (“hollow”), from Latin cavus.

parole.significato: A mineral with orthorhombic crystals, SrSO₄, colourless or white with blue and sometimes red shades.
parole.testo: From Italian celestina (“sky-blue”), from Latin caelestīnus, &c.

parole.significato: A harpsichord.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian cembalo, from Latin. Doublet of cymbal.

parole.significato: To seek; to search.
parole.testo: From Italian cercare (“to look for”), from Late Latin circāre (“to traverse, go about”), from Latin circa (“around, near, about”), circus (“a circular line or orbit”), from Ancient Greek κίρκος (kírkos, “circle, ring”).

parole.significato: A hilly geographic region in central Tuscany, Italy, famous for red wines.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian chianti, after Chianti, its area of production. Through Latin from the Etruscan 𐌂𐌋𐌀𐌍𐌕𐌄 (clante).

parole.significato: A guide who accompanies visitors and sightseers to museums, galleries, etc., and explains matters of archaeological, an…
parole.testo: 1726, from Italian cicerone (surface analysis cicero + -one (augmentative)), from Latin Cicerōnem, form of Cicerō, agnomen of Marcus Tullius Cicero), the Roman orator, from cicer (“chickpea”) from Proto-Indo-European *ḱiker- (“pea”). Possibly humorous reference to loquaciousness of guides.

parole.significato: Synonym of Poor Clare: a nun of the Order of Saint Clare.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian Clarissa, from Medieval Latin Clarissa; see there for more. Popularized in English by Samuel Richardson's 1748 novel Clarissa. Doublet of Clarisse.

parole.significato: A passage that brings a movement or piece to a conclusion through prolongation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian coda (literally “tail”), from Latin cauda. Doublet of queue and cola.

parole.significato: The tow obtained from flax or hemp.
parole.testo: Diminutive from Italian coda, from Latin cauda (“a tail”).

parole.significato: Someone possessing superior or specialized knowledge in a particular field.
parole.testo: From obsolete Italian cognoscente (modern Italian conoscente) from Latin cognōscere (“to know”).

parole.significato: Florid or fancy passages in vocal music.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian coloratura, from Late Latin colōrātūra, from colōrāre (“to colour”).

parole.significato: Affected wit; a witty turn of phrase; a conceit.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian concetto, from Latin conceptus. See conceit and concept, which are doublets.

parole.significato: The person who prepares the materials to be made into glass, and/or works and tempers them.
parole.testo: From Italian conciatore, from conciare (“to adjust, dress”), from Latin comptus, past participle. See compt (adjective).

parole.significato: A mercenary military leader from 14th-century Italy and later in other parts of Europe.
parole.testo: From Italian condottiere, from Latin conductus (“assembled, collected”).

parole.significato: A counselor or advisor, especially to Mafia bosses.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian consigliere, from Italian consiglio (“advice", counsel”), from Latin cōnsilium (“council”). Entered the popular English lexicon through Mario Puzo's “Godfather” novels and the subsequent films made from them.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or resulting from a consortium.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian consorziale, from consorzio, from the Latin consortium; compare the French consortial.

parole.significato: The position of a human figure whose hips and legs are twisted away from the direction of the head and shoulders; (coun…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian contrapposto (“contrasting; opposing”, adjective), the past participle of contrapporre (“to set against, counter”), from Latin contrāpōnere, the present active infinitive of contrāpōnō (“to oppose; to place opposite”), from contrā (“against; contrary to”) + pōnō (“to place, put

parole.significato: A trumpet-like wind instrument used in European music of the medieval, Renaissance, and Baroque periods.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian cornetto, a diminutive of corno (“horn”), from Latin cornū.

parole.significato: French horn
parole.testo: From Italian corno, from Latin cornu (“horn”). Doublet of corn (“callus”), cornu, and horn.

parole.significato: A cuckold.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian cornuto, from Latin cornūtus (“horned”).

parole.significato: One who makes another person into a cuckold.
parole.testo: From Italian cornuto, from Latin cornūtus, from cornu. By surface analysis, cornute + -or.

parole.significato: A series of sonnets linked together such that the last word of each is the first word of the next.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian corona.

parole.significato: To cheat; to defraud; to deceive, usually by small arts, or in a pitiful way.
parole.testo: Perhaps from obsolete Italian cozzonare (“to cheat”), from cozzone (“middleman, broker”), from Latin cōciō (“dealer”).

parole.significato: A superior kind of violin, formerly made at Cremona in Italy.
parole.testo: From Italian Cremona, from Latin Cremōna.

parole.significato: A dome-shaped ornamental structure located on top of a larger roof or dome.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian cupola, from Latin cūpula (“little tub”); from Latin cūpa, cuppa (“cup”); named for its resemblance to a cup turned over. Doublet of cupula.

parole.significato: Of a horse or, by extension, another animal: to leap about, to frolic.
parole.testo: From Italian corvetta, diminutive of corva, an early form of curva (“curve”), from Latin curva, feminine of curvus (“bent, curved”).

parole.significato: Disused; out of use.
parole.testo: Probably via Italian, from Latin dēsuētus (“unused”), past participle of dēsuēscō (“to disuse”), from dē- + suēscō (“to make use of”).

parole.significato: An amateur, someone who dabbles in a field out of casual interest rather than as a profession or serious interest.
parole.testo: From Italian dilettante, present participle of dilettare (“to delight”), from Latin dēlectāre (“to delight”).

parole.significato: The science of authenticating, dating, and interpreting old official documents.
parole.testo: Probably from Italian or Ecclesiastical Latin diplomatica.

parole.significato: To part, separate.
parole.testo: From Italian dispartire and its source, Latin dispartire.

parole.significato: A finger-operated key for raising the pitch of a guitar by a semitone.
parole.testo: From Italian ditale, from Latin digitus (“finger”).

parole.significato: That which was stated before, the aforesaid, the above, the same, likewise.
parole.testo: First attested in 1625. From regional Italian ditto, variant of detto, past participle of dire (“to say”), from Latin dīcō (“to say, to speak”). Not related to English dittography. The specific meaning of making copies of paper comes from ditto machine, a genericization from the brand name of a spir

parole.significato: Any female celebrity, usually a well known singer or actress.
parole.testo: From Italian diva (“diva, goddess”), from Latin dīva (“goddess”), female of dīvus (“divine, divine one; notably a deified mortal”), from Old Latin deivā, from Proto-Italic *deiwā (“goddess”), feminine of *deiwos (“god”), from Proto-Indo-European *deywós (“god”).

parole.significato: composition that has several short movements, a style that composers started to use in the 18th century.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian, from divertire (“to amuse, to entertain”), from Latin dīvertere.

parole.significato: A male diva; a man with the traits characteristic of a typical diva.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian divo.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a doge.
parole.testo: From Italian dogale (whence also Medieval Latin dogalis), from Late Latin ducalis (“ducal”). Doublet of ducal.

parole.significato: The office or dignity of a doge.
parole.testo: From Italian dogato, from Latin ducatus. Doublet of ducat and duchy.

parole.significato: Describing the Copper Age, which occurred between the Neolithic and the Bronze Age.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian eneolitico, from Latin aeneus (“copper, bronze”).

parole.significato: A syllable used in solfège to represent the fourth diatonic (or sixth chromatic) note of a major scale.
parole.testo: From Glover's solmization, from Middle English fa (“fourth degree or note of Guido of Arezzo's hexachordal scales”), Italian fa in the solmization of Guido of Arezzo, from the first syllable of Latin famulī (“servants”) in the lyrics of the scale-ascending hymn Ut queant laxis by Paulus Deacon.

parole.significato: A form of instrumental composition with a free structure and improvisational characteristics; specifically, one combini…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian fantasia (“imagination, fancy, fantasy; improvisational song”), from Latin phantasia (“fancy, fantasy; imagination”), borrowed from Ancient Greek φᾰντᾰσῐ́ᾱ (phăntăsĭ́ā, “appearance; presentation; pageantry; perception; image”), see that entry for further details. Doublet of fan

parole.significato: fantastic
parole.testo: From Italian fantastico (“fantastic”), from Late Latin phantasticus (“imaginary”). Doublet of fantastic and fantastique.

parole.significato: A bundle or sheaf.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian fascio.

parole.significato: copper sulphide, used to colour glass.
parole.testo: From Italian ferretto di Spagna, diminutive of ferro (“iron”), from Latin ferrum.

parole.significato: A sudden or unexpected failure.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian fiasco (“bottle, flask”), from Late Latin flasca, flascō (“bottle, container”), from Frankish *flaskā (“bottle, flask”) from Proto-Germanic *flaskǭ (“bottle”); see flask. “Failure” sense comes through French faire fiasco from Italian theatrical slang far fiasco (literally “to m

parole.significato: a fig; an insignificant trifle
parole.testo: From Italian fico (“a fig”), from Latin fīcus. Doublet of fig.

parole.significato: The grand end of something, especially of a show or piece of music.
parole.testo: From Italian finale (“ending”), from Late Latin fīnālis, from Latin fīnis (“end; boundary, limit”). Doublet of final.

parole.significato: Finished; over with; done.
parole.testo: From Italian finito (“finished”), from Latin fīnītus. Doublet of finite.

parole.significato: (disused nomenclature) Promethium.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian florentium, florenzio, from Latin Florentia (“Florence”) + -ium (“metallic element”).

parole.significato: A flatbread similar in style, composition, and texture to modern pizza doughs and topped with herbs, cheese and other p…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Italian focaccia, from Late Latin focācium (via its plural focācia), derived from Latin focus (“hearth”). Doublet of fougasse and pagash. Cognate with Sicilian fugazza, Serbo-Croatian pogača (“unleavened bread”).

parole.significato: A cool, refreshing state of the air; coolness, duskiness, shade.
parole.testo: From Italian fresco, from Vulgar Latin *friscum, from Proto-Germanic *friskaz. Doublet of fresh and frisk.

parole.significato: A large, broad-brimmed, tasseled hat worn by Catholic clergy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian galero, from Latin galērum.

parole.significato: An old Venetian coin of little value.
parole.testo: From Italian gazeta, gazzetta, probably diminutive of Latin gaza (“royal treasure”).

parole.significato: gelato, Italian style ice-cream; a serving of gelato, often in a cone.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian gelati, the plural form of gelato, from Latin gelātus, derived from gelū (“frost, chill”), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“cold”).

parole.significato: An Italian variant of ice cream made from milk and sugar, combined with other flavourings. The ingredients are supercoo…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian gelato (“ice cream”), from Latin gelātus, derived from gelū (“frost, chill”), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“cold”).

parole.significato: Merry; playful.
parole.testo: From Italian giocoso, from Latin iocōsus.

parole.significato: A tempo mark directing that a passage is to be played in a grand and noble style
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian grandioso, from Latin grandis (“great, grand”) (English grand). Doublet of grandiose.

parole.significato: graceful, flowing
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian grazioso (“graceful”), from Latin grātiōsus (“agreeable, popular”), from grātia (“grace”). Doublet of gracioso and gracious.

parole.significato: A small cave.
parole.testo: From Italian grotta, from Vulgar Latin grupta, from Classical Latin crypta. Doublet of crypt. The Philippine sense is from the holy cave in Lourdes, France.

parole.significato: An Italian or (especially) Italian-American man, especially a stereotypical working-class or lower-class, usually urban…
parole.testo: From Italian Guido, a male given name. Doublet of Guido, Guy, and guy.

parole.significato: Enthusiasm; enjoyment, vigor.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian gusto, from Latin gustus (“taste”). Doublet of cost (see Etymology 3 there).

parole.significato: The style of a prince, princess or someone of equivalent rank.
parole.testo: Calque of Italian altezza, from Late Latin altitia, from altus + -itia, equivalent to high + -ness. See highness for formation of the English term.

parole.significato: The top part of a column, pillar, pier, wall, etc. that supports an arch.
parole.testo: From Italian imposta, from Latin imposta.

parole.significato: Without being known; in an assumed character, or under an assumed title; in disguise.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian incognito, from Latin incognitus (“unknown”), from in- (“not”) + cognitus (“known”), perfect passive participle of cognoscere.

parole.significato: A place or situation resembling Hell.
parole.testo: From Italian inferno (“hell”), from Latin infernus (“of the lower regions”), inferna (“the lower regions”); see infernal. The meaning "big fire" came as a figurative use from the traditional idea of hellfire.

parole.significato: To render or demonstrate to be invalid; to invalidate or disprove.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian inficiare + English -ate (suffix forming verbs), from Medieval Latin īnficior, alteration of Classical Latin īnfitior (“to deny, contradict”), from *īnfitiae (“denial”) (see īnfitiās eō), from fateor (“to admit, acknowledge”). Presumably originally a mistranslation by Italian s

parole.significato: An acute contagious disease of the upper airways and lungs, caused by a virus, which rapidly spreads around the world i…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian influenza (“influence”), from Latin influentia. Doublet of influence.

parole.significato: Cheating; deception.
parole.testo: From Italian ingannazione, nominal form derived from ingannare (“deceive, cheat, betray”) from Vulgar Latin ingannāre, from Latin gannō.

parole.significato: To bring oneself into favour with someone by flattering or trying to please them; to insinuate oneself; to worm one's w…
parole.testo: First attested in 1622. From Italian ingraziare or Medieval Latin *ingratiatus, from Latin in grātiam (“for the favor of”).

parole.significato: A syllable used in solfège to represent the sixth note of a major scale.
parole.testo: From Glover's solmization, from Middle English la (“sixth degree or note of Guido of Arezzo's hexachordal scales”), Italian la in the solmization of Guido of Arezzo, from the first syllable of Latin labiī (“lip's”) in the lyrics of the scale-ascending hymn Ut queant laxis by Paulus Deacon.

parole.significato: A flat sheet of pasta.
parole.testo: From Italian lasagna (and its plural lasagne), possibly from Vulgar Latin *lasania, from Latin lasanum (“cooking pot”), from Ancient Greek λάσανον (lásanon, “trivet or stand for a pot”). Others argue the Italian lasagna originally derived from the Arabic لَوْزِينَج (lawzīnaj, “almond cake”).

parole.significato: A drink of coffee made from espresso and steamed milk, generally topped with foam.
parole.testo: Ellipsis of caffè latte, from Italian caffellatte, ultimately from Latin lac, lactis.

parole.significato: A balance.
parole.testo: From Italian lance, Latin lanx, lancis (“plate, scale of a balance”); compare balance.

parole.significato: A place reserved for people with infectious diseases (especially leprosy or plague) to live on a long-term basis.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian lazzareto (archaic), lazzaretto, lazzeretto, from lazzaro (“leper”) + -etto (diminutive or meliorative suffix). Lazzaro is derived from Medieval Latin lazarus (“leper”), from Lazarus, from Ancient Greek Λᾱ́ζᾱρος (Lā́zāros), from Hebrew אֶלְעָזָר ('el'azár, literally “God has he

parole.significato: Smoothly, in a connected manner.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian legato, past participle of legare (“to tie up, tie together, to bind”), learned borrowing from Latin ligō (“tie, bind”). Doublet of ligate.

parole.significato: The text of a dramatic musical work, such as an opera.
parole.testo: From Italian libretto, diminutive of libro (“book”), from Latin liber (“book”).

parole.significato: Part of the sea by a beach sectioned off for swimming and other aquatic activities.
parole.testo: After Lido (Lido di Venezia), an island with a long beach in Venice, Italy, site of Europe’s first modern beach resort (1857), from Italian lido (“beach, shore”), from Latin litus (“shore”) (hence also English littoral (“of the shore”)). The name is aspirational, evoking glamorous Venice; compare Ve

parole.significato: The basic unit of currency in Turkey.
parole.testo: From Italian lira, from Latin lībra (partly via Turkish lira, Arabic لِيرَة (līra), Maltese lira, Greek λίρα (líra), and Hebrew לִירָה (“lirá”), all of which are originally from the Italian). Doublet of arratel, libbra, Libra, libra, litra, litre, livre, and rottol.

parole.significato: A song for a small number of unaccompanied voices; from 13th century Italy.
parole.testo: From Italian madrigale, from Latin mātrīcālis.

parole.significato: A master in some art, especially a composer or conductor.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian maestro, from Latin magistrum (“master”). Doublet of magister, master, and meister.

parole.significato: major
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian maggiore.

parole.significato: A public declaration of principles, policies, or intentions, especially that of a political party.
parole.testo: Since the mid 17th century, from Italian manifesto, from manifestare + -o, from Latin manifestō (“to make public”), from Latin manus + an uncertain second element. Doublet of manifest.

parole.significato: Disgusting, repulsive.
parole.testo: Via Polari, from Italian mancare (“to be lacking”), from Latin mancus (“maimed”). See above.

parole.significato: A sleeveless, knee-length vestment open at the front which is worn by Roman Catholic prelates.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian mantelletta, from mantello (“cloak, mantle”) + -etta (from -etto (diminutive suffix)), probably from Late Latin mantelletum (“a short, sleeveless cape or cloak; a mantlet”). Doublet of mantlet.

parole.significato: A European cultivar of the wild cherry (Prunus cerasus), that bears bright red fruit used for making maraschino.
parole.testo: From Italian marasca, from amarasca, from amaro (“bitter”), from Latin amārus (“bitter”).

parole.significato: An Italian marquis.
parole.testo: Italian, from Late Latin marchensis.

parole.significato: A renowned traveler.
parole.testo: After Marco Polo (1254–1324), Venetian merchant, whose travels were documented in a book that introduced Europeans to Central Asia and China. The Italian name is from Latin Marcus + Paulus.

parole.significato: Strongly accented, or hammered out; used of notes played on bowed string instruments, handbells, or the piano.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian martellato (“hammered”), from martellare (“to hammer, throb”), from martello (“hammer”), related to Latin martulus, marculus (“small hammer”), diminutive of marcus (“hammer”).

parole.significato: The solfeggio syllable used to indicate the flat of the third note of a major scale.
parole.testo: From mi (“third note of a major scale”) + -e (“flat”), from Glover's solmization, Italian mi in the solmization of Guido of Arezzo, from the first syllable of Latin mīra in the lyrics of the scale-ascending hymn Ut queant laxis by Paulus Deacon.

parole.significato: The third degree of the diatonic scale.
parole.testo: From Italian mediante, from Latin mediānt- (“being in the middle”), present active participle of mediō (“to be in the middle”), from medius (“middle”), from Proto-Italic *meðios, from Proto-Indo-European *medʰyo- (“between”).

parole.significato: A syllable used in sol-fa (solfège) to represent the third note of a major scale.
parole.testo: From Glover's solmization, from Middle English mi (“third degree or note of Guido of Arezzo's hexachordal scales”), Italian mi in the solmization of Guido of Arezzo, from the first syllable of Latin mīra (“miracles; the miraculous”) in the lyrics of the scale-ascending hymn Ut queant laxis by Paulus

parole.significato: An optical instrument used for observing small objects.
parole.testo: From New Latin microscopium and Italian microscopio, from Ancient Greek μικρός (mikrós, “small”) + σκοπέω (skopéō, “to look at”), equivalent to micro- + -scope.

parole.significato: Any of many thick Italian vegetable soups.
parole.testo: Directly from Italian minestrone, from minestra (“soup”, ultimately from Latin ministrō) + -one (augmentative suffix).

parole.significato: A preparatory sketch or study for a painting or other artwork.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian modello.

parole.significato: A mordent (embellishment resembling a trill).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian mordente, from Latin mordēns, from mordēre.

parole.significato: A smooth-textured Italian pork sausage with lumps of fat, flavoured with spices; eaten cold.
parole.testo: From Italian mortadella, from diminutive of Latin murtatum (“sausage seasoned with myrtle berries”), from myrtatum, from myrtus, from Ancient Greek μύρτος (múrtos).

parole.significato: A personal slogan.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian motto (“a word, a saying”), from Latin muttum (“a mutter, a grunt”), late 16th c. Doublet of mot.

parole.significato: Soft Italian or Italian-style cheese made from cow's or buffalo's milk and commonly used as a pizza topping and in sala…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian mozzarella, from mozzare (“to cut off”), from Latin mutilare. The meaning of money derives from the early Bay Area hip-hop scene since early and is found for various food terms, including cheddar and cheese.

parole.significato: Pertaining to nutmeg.
parole.testo: From Italian miristico, from Late Latin myristicus (“fragrant”); the form Myristica first used by Linnaeus as a genus name for the nutmeg tree. From Ancient Greek μυριστικός (muristikós, “fragrant”), from Ancient Greek μυρίζω (murízō, “to anoint”), from μύρον (múron, “unguent, perfume”). Compare myr

parole.significato: Any of various black metal alloys, made of sulphur with copper, silver or lead, used to create decorative designs on ot…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian niello, from Latin nigellus (“blackish”).

parole.significato: A grandfather, especially one with Italian ancestry.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian nonno.

parole.significato: A nocturne.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian notturno (“nocturnal, nightly”), from Latin nocturnus, from noctū (“by night”), from nox (“night”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts. Doublet of nocturne.

parole.significato: A work of prose fiction, longer than a novella.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian novella, from Latin novella, feminine of novellus. Doublet of novella.

parole.significato: To act as an obstacle to; to impede, obstruct.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian ostacolare, as if from a Latin *obstāculātus. Equivalent to obstacle + -ate.

parole.significato: A man.
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from Italian uomo (“man”). Doublet of gome, hombre, homo, and ombre.

parole.significato: A musical composition, often based on a religious theme; similar to opera but with no costume, scenery or acting.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian oratorio (“oratorical”), from Latin ōrātōrius. Doublet of oratory.

parole.significato: A form of pasta the size and shape of grains of rice or barley; often used in soups.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian orzo (“barley”), from Latin hordeum, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰr̥sdeyom (“bristly”). Doublet of orgeat and horchata.

parole.significato: A classical convex moulding carved with an egg and dart ornament.
parole.testo: From Italian ovolo, from Latin ōvum (“egg”). Doublet of ovule.

parole.significato: A patron; a protector.
parole.testo: From Italian padrone, from Latin patronus. Doublet of patron, Patronus, patroon, and pattern.

parole.significato: A large, palatial urban building in Italy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian palazzo, from Latin palātium (“palace, large residence”), from Palātium (“Palatine”), one of the seven hills of Rome, where aristocrats built large homes. Doublet of palace and Pfalz.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Palermo on the island of Sicily in Italy.
parole.testo: From Italian palermitano, from Latin Panormitānus. By surface analysis, Palermo + -itan. Doublet of Panormitan.

parole.significato: A person who furthers the illicit love-affairs of others; a pimp or procurer.
parole.testo: From Middle English pandare, from Chaucer’s character Pandare (in Troilus and Criseyde; see also Shakespeare’s Troilus and Cressida), from Italian Pandaro (found in Boccaccio), from Latin Pandarus (found in Greek mythology), from Ancient Greek Πάνδαρος (Pándaros).

parole.significato: Any of very many vines, in North America and elsewhere, of the genus Passiflora that bear edible fruit called passion f…
parole.testo: Calque of Italian fior della Passione or Latin flōs Passiōnis; after the appearance and number of its various parts, thought to be symbolic of Christ's passion.

parole.significato: Dough made from wheat and water and sometimes mixed with egg and formed into various shapes; often sold in dried form a…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian pasta (“paste; pasta, noodles”), from Late Latin pasta (“dough, pastry cake, paste”), from Ancient Greek παστά (pastá, “barley porridge”), neuter plural of παστός (pastós, “sprinkled with salt”), from Ancient Greek πάσσω (pássō, “to sprinkle”). Doublet of paste.

parole.significato: A Greek dish made with cheese, chopped meat and pasta, resembling lasagna.
parole.testo: From Italian pasticcio (“hodge-podge”), from Vulgar Latin *pasticium, from *pastīcius (“of dough”), from Latin pasta (“dough, pastry cake, paste”), from Ancient Greek παστά (pastá, “barley porridge”), from παστός (pastós, “sprinkled with salt”). Doublet of pastiche.

parole.significato: A peacock.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian pavone. From oblique stem of Latin pāvō, pāvōnis (“peacock, peafowl”).

parole.significato: A disease characterised by skin lesions and mental confusion, primarily caused by a niacin deficiency.
parole.testo: From Italian pellagra, from Latin pellis (“skin”) + Ancient Greek ἄγρα (ágra, “seizure, attack, catching”).

parole.significato: The presence of traces of a previous work in an artistic or literary work; especially (painting) an image which has bee…
parole.testo: [Alt: A blue-tinted painting of a man's bent neck, with a faint image of a woman's face in its background] Learned borrowing from Italian pentimento (“repentance, penance, penitence; remorse; change of opinion; correction; traces of a previous image or work in an artwork”), from pentìrsi (“to repent

parole.significato: A framework in the form of a passageway of columns that supports a trelliswork roof; used to support and train climbing…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian pergola, from Latin pergula.

parole.significato: A sauce, especially for pasta, originating from the Genoa region in Italy, made from basil, garlic, pine nuts, olive oi…
parole.testo: Appears 1850 in Cottage economy, attributed to William Cobbett (but not found in any editions published during his life). From Italian pesto, from Latin pistus (“crushed, pounded”), from Latin pīnsō (“to pound, beat, crush”). Cognate to pestle.

parole.significato: A deciduous tree (Pistacia vera) grown in parts of Asia for its drupaceous fruit.
parole.testo: From Italian pistacchio (1590s), from Latin pistācium (“pistachio”), from Ancient Greek πιστάκιον (pistákion), from πιστάκη (pistákē, “pistachio tree”), of Iranian origin. Compare Middle English pistace (from Middle French pistace, pistache), Northern Kurdish pisteq, Persian پسته (peste), Middle Per

parole.significato: A chief magistrate of various Italian republics and city-states in the Middle Ages.
parole.testo: From Italian podesta, from Latin potestas (“power; powerful one”). Doublet of poustie. See potent.

parole.significato: Any of various types and consistencies of a starchy accompaniment to a meal made from coarse maize-meal porridge, somet…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian polenta.

parole.significato: Glassmaker's ashes; a kind of potash or pearlash, brought from the Levant and Syria, used in the manufacture of fine gl…
parole.testo: From Italian polverino, from Latin pulvis (“dust”). Doublet of pulvinus.

parole.significato: In an unconnected manner, as opposed to legato, but not as short as staccato.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian portato, past participle of portare (“to bring, carry, bear”), from Latin portō.

parole.significato: A case for carrying papers, drawings, photographs, maps and other flat documents.
parole.testo: From Italian portafoglio; cognate with French portefeuille (“folder, wallet”), from Latin portāre (“to carry”) and folium (“sheet”). The meaning "collection of responsibilities" came by extension in the 1930s.

parole.significato: A porch, or a small space with a roof supported by columns, serving as the entrance to a building.
parole.testo: From Italian portico, from Latin porticus (“porch”), from porta (“gate”). Doublet of porch, portego, and porticus.

parole.significato: The large, mature form of the crimini mushroom (Agaricus bisporus)
parole.testo: In use by 1985. Uncertain origin. Possibly a marketing name; possibly from dialectal Italian pratarolo (“meadow mushroom”), ultimately from Latin pratum (“meadow”). It has also said to be named after Portobello Road in London, which originally led to the Porto Bello House.

parole.significato: A type of volcanic ash used for mortar or for cement which sets under water.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian pozz(u)olana, earth of Pozzuoli, a town near Naples, itself from Latin Puteoli, ultimately from the verb puteō (“stink”).

parole.significato: most important
parole.testo: Derived from Italian prima, derived from Latin prīma.

parole.significato: One employed to procure supplies, as for an army, a steamer, etc.; a purveyor; one who provides for another.
parole.testo: From Italian proveditore, provveditore, from provedere, Latin providere. See provide. Doublet of purveyor and provedore.

parole.significato: A dosseret shaped like an inverted pyramid, placed between the column capital and the arch base.
parole.testo: Italian pulvino, from Latin pulvīnus (“cushion, pillow, bolster”). Doublet of pillow, polverine, pulvinus, pulvillus, and pulvinulus, as well as others.

parole.significato: A representation, especially in Renaissance or Baroque art, of a small, naked, often winged (usually male) child; a che…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian putto (“cupid, putto; boy”), from Latin putus (“boy”), a variant of pūsus (“(little) boy”), from puer (“boy, lad; child”), from Proto-Italic *puweros, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂w- (“few, little; smallness”). The plural form putti is also borrowed from Italian put

parole.significato: The interval of a fifteenth, a double octave.
parole.testo: From Italian quindecima, from Latin quindecima (“15th”), from quindecim (“15”).

parole.significato: Of, from, or concerning Ravenna, a major city in Italy.
parole.testo: From Ravenna + -ate (adjective-forming suffix); an anglicized form of Italian ravennate and Latin Ravennās through incorrectly associated endings (see Latin -ās).

parole.significato: A syllable used in solfège to represent the second note of a major scale.
parole.testo: From Glover's solmization, from Middle English re (“second degree or note of Guido of Arezzo's hexachordal scales”), Italian re in the solmization of Guido of Arezzo, from the first syllable of Latin resonāre (“made to resound”) in the lyrics of the scale-ascending hymn Ut queant laxis by Paulus Dea

parole.significato: dialogue, in an opera etc, that, rather than being sung as an aria, is reproduced with the rhythms of normal speech, of…
parole.testo: From Italian recitativo, from recitare, from Latin recitō.

parole.significato: A method of sculpture or other artwork in which shapes or figures protrude from a flat background.
parole.testo: From Italian rilievo, from rilevare (“to raise”), from Latin relevō (“to raise”).

parole.significato: An exact copy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian replica, derived from Latin replicare (“to fold or bend back; to reply”). Doublet of reply and replicate.

parole.significato: A soft Italian unsalted whey cheese resembling cottage cheese.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian ricotta (literally “cooked again”), from Latin recocta.

parole.significato: A small stream; a streamlet; a gill.
parole.testo: From Italian rivoletto, diminutive of rivolo (“trickle, little stream”), diminutive of rivo (“stream, brook, creek”), ultimately from Latin rīvulus, diminutive of rīvus. By surface analysis, Latin rīvus + -ule + -et.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Rota.
parole.testo: From Italian and Latin Rota (“an ecclesiastical appellate court in the Catholic Church”) + -al (“forming adjectives”), under the influence of Latin rotālis.

parole.significato: A large cured meat sausage of Italian origin, served in slices.
parole.testo: From Italian salami, plural of salame (“salami”), from sale (“salt”), from Latin sal.

parole.significato: A somersault.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian salto (“jump, leap”), from Latin saltus (“jump, leap”). Compare German Salto, French salto, Dutch salto, Hungarian szaltó. Doublet of saltus.

parole.significato: An Italian liqueur made from elderberries and flavoured with licorice, traditionally served with 3 coffee beans that re…
parole.testo: ] Borrowed from Italian sambuca, from Latin sambūcus (“elder tree”), due to a similar 19th century liquor flavored with elderflower. Modern sambuca, which doesn't necessarily have elderberry, started being marketed in 1971.

parole.significato: Chiefly in scarper the letty: to depart quickly or run away from (a place); to flee.
parole.testo: The verb is probably borrowed from Italian scappare (“to run away, escape, flee”), from Vulgar Latin *excappāre (“to escape”), from Latin ex- (prefix meaning ‘away; out’) + cappa (“(Late Latin) cape, cloak (usually with a hood); (Medieval Latin) cap; headwear”) (further etymology uncertain, probably

parole.significato: To perform a cursory investigation of; scope out.
parole.testo: From Italian scopo (“purpose”), from Latin scopus (“target”), from Ancient Greek σκοπός (skopós), from σκέπτομαι (sképtomai), from Proto-Indo-European *speḱ-. Etymologically related to skeptic and spectrum.

parole.significato: A silver coin and unit of currency of various Italian states from the 16th to the 19th centuries.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian scudo (“a crown, a dollar, a shield”), from Latin scutum (“a shield”). Compare the doublets scute, escudo, scutum, and écu.

parole.significato: An enclosed windowed chair suitable for a single occupant, carried by at least two porters, in equal numbers in front a…
parole.testo: The sense of "windowed chair" was first used by Sir Sanders Duncombe in 1634, possibly from a southern Italian dialect of Italian sede (“seat”), from Latin sedes. The "motorcar" sense was first recorded in 1912 in North America.

parole.significato: The sign 𝄋, indicating the start of a passage of music to be repeated.
parole.testo: From Italian segno, from Latin signum. Doublet of sign.

parole.significato: To move smoothly from one state or subject to another.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian segue (“it follows”), from seguire (“to follow”), from Latin sequor; originally a term used in a musical score to indicate that the next movement or passage is to follow without a break. Cognate with Spanish seguir. Doublet of sue. Related to suit and sequence.

parole.significato: A musical note four beats long in 4/4 time; a whole note (US)
parole.testo: From Italian semibreve, ultimately from Latin semi- (“half”) and Latin brevis (“short”).

parole.significato: semolina
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian semola, from Latin simila (“fine flour”). Doublet of semla and semel.

parole.significato: A palace of a sultan.
parole.testo: From Italian serraglio, from Vulgar Latin *serrāculum, from a late form of Latin serāre (“lock up, close”), from sera (“lock, bolt”). The Italian word was used (because of phonetic similarity) to translate Turkish saray (“palace”). Compare serai, serail.

parole.significato: A piece of music composed for six voices or six instruments; a sextet or sestuor.
parole.testo: From Italian sestetto, from sesto (“sixth”), Latin sextus, from sex (“six”).

parole.significato: A syllable used in solfège to represent the seventh note of a major scale.
parole.testo: From Middle English si (“seventh degree or note of Guido of Arezzo's hexachordal scales”), Italian si in the solmization of Guido of Arezzo, from the initials of Latin Sāncte Iohannēs (“Saint John (the Baptist)”) in the lyrics of the scale-ascending hymn Ut queant laxis by Paulus Deacon; thus, also

parole.significato: A symphony.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian sinfonia. Doublet of symphonia, symphony, tsampouna, and zampogna.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Pope Sixtus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian sistino, from New Latin sixtīnus, from the Medieval Latin name Sixtus, from Latin Sextus.

parole.significato: A deep blue pigment made from powdered glass mixed with cobalt oxide.
parole.testo: A borrowing from Italian smalto, from Medieval Latin smaltum, from Frankish *smalt, from Proto-Germanic *smeltaną (“to melt, smelt”). A doublet of smalto.

parole.significato: A syllable used in solfège to represent the fifth note of a major scale.
parole.testo: Shortened from sol, to make it an open syllable for uniformity with the rest of the scale, from Glover's solmization, from Middle English sol (“fifth degree or note of Guido of Arezzo's hexachordal scales”), Italian sol in the solmization of Guido of Arezzo, from the first syllable of Latin solve (“

parole.significato: In a movable-do or tonic sol-fa system: the fifth step in a scale, preceded by fa and followed by la.
parole.testo: From Glover's solmization, from Middle English sol (“fifth degree or note of Guido of Arezzo's hexachordal scales”), Italian sol in the solmization of Guido of Arezzo, from the first syllable of Latin solve (“wash away”) in the lyrics of the scale-ascending hymn Ut queant laxis by Paulus Deacon.

parole.significato: An Italian coin, formerly one-twentieth of a lira.
parole.testo: From Italian soldo, from Latin solidum. Doublet of sol, sold, solid, solidus, sou, and xu.

parole.significato: A piece of music for one performer.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian solo, from Latin sōlus, probably related to se (“himself”).

parole.significato: A musical composition for one or a few instruments, one of which is frequently a piano, in three or four movements that…
parole.testo: From Italian sonata, from the feminine past participle of sonare (modern suonare), from Latin sonāre (“to make sound”). Doublet of sounded.

parole.significato: The musical part higher in pitch than alto, typically encompassing the range of the treble clef.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian soprano, from Vulgar Latin *superānus, adjective from preposition Latin super (“above”). Doublet of sovereign, from the same Latin root via Old French.

parole.significato: A kind of Italian walnut.
parole.testo: From Italian Sorrento, from Latin Surrentum, of uncertain origin.

parole.significato: A playing card marked with the symbol ♠.
parole.testo: Probably from Italian spade, plural of spada (“the ace of spades”, literally “sword, spade”), from earlier *spata, from Latin spatha, from Ancient Greek σπᾰ́θη (spắthē). Cognate with Etymology 1. So called for the shape, though what the shape was exactly meant to represent has been debated.

parole.significato: To serve (someone) spaghetti (noun noun 1 sense 1).
parole.testo: The noun is borrowed from Italian spaghetti, the plural of spaghetto (“strand of spaghetti”), from spago (“cord, string, twine; thread”) + -etto (diminutive suffix). Spago is derived from Latin spagus (“twine”), probably from Ancient Greek σφάκος (sphákos, “apple sage (Salvia pomifera)”), probably f

parole.significato: A unit of a poem, written or printed as a paragraph; equivalent to a verse.
parole.testo: From Italian stanza, from Vulgar Latin *stantia (“standing, stopping-place”), from Latin stāns, stantis, from stō, stāre, from Proto-Italic *staēō, from Proto-Indo-European *sth₂éh₁yeti, stative verb from *steh₂- (whence English stand). Doublet of stance.

parole.significato: An artist’s or photographer’s workshop or the room in which an artist works.
parole.testo: From Italian studio (“room for study”), from Latin studium. Doublet of study and etude.

parole.significato: Suddenly, abruptly.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian subito.

parole.significato: An officer on board a merchant ship who is in charge of the cargo and its sale; also, if there are two of such officers…
parole.testo: From English supra- (prefix meaning ‘above, over’) + borrowed from Italian sopracargo, a dialectal form of sopraccarico, from sopra- (prefix meaning ‘above, over’) + carico (“cargo”) (from caricare (“to load; to take aboard”), from Late Latin carricāre, the present active infinitive of carricō (“to

parole.significato: A frequency or rate.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian tempo, from Latin tempus (“time”). Doublet of tense. (truck or cargo van): A genericized trademark, originally associated with the manufacturer Vidal & Sohn Tempo-Werke GmbH.

parole.significato: A style of painting using very pronounced chiaroscuro, with darkness a dominating feature of the image.
parole.testo: From Italian tenebrismo, from tenebroso + -ismo, from Latin tenebrōsus (“dark, gloomy”).

parole.significato: A composition in three voice parts, or the vocal (or, rarely, instrumental) trio.
parole.testo: From Italian terzetto, diminutive of Italian terzo (“the third”), from Latin tertius. See tierce.

parole.significato: A syllable used in solfège to represent the seventh note of a major scale.
parole.testo: Coined by English music educator Sarah Anna Glover in 1812 as an alteration of si for her solmization, made so that every note of solfège would begin with a different letter, from Middle English si (“seventh degree or note of Guido of Arezzo's hexachordal scales”), Italian si in the solmization of G

parole.significato: The set of precision kettledrums in an orchestra.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian timpani, plural of timpano (“drum”), from Latin tympanum (“drum”), from Ancient Greek τύμπανον (túmpanon), from τύπτω (túptō, “to strike, to hit”). Doublet of tympanum, timbre, timbal, and tymbal.

parole.significato: A game resembling bagatelle, played on a special oblong board or table with a curved upper end, a set of numbered compa…
parole.testo: From Italian Tivoli, from Latin Tībur.

parole.significato: A spit of sand linking an island to the mainland (or to another island), formed by longshore drift.
parole.testo: From Italian tombolo (“pillow”), from Latin tumulus (“mound”), from tumeō (“to swell”). Doublet of tumulus.

parole.significato: A round picture or other work of art.
parole.testo: From Italian tondo, from ritondo, rotondo (“round”), from Latin rotundus. Doublet of round.

parole.significato: The main part of the (human) body that extends from the neck to the groin, excluding the head and limbs.
parole.testo: From Italian torso, from Late Latin tursus, from Latin thyrsus, from Ancient Greek θύρσος (thúrsos, “Bacchic staff”). Doublet of thyrse, thyrsus, and torse.

parole.significato: An Italian cake.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian torta, from Latin turta, thought to derive from Latin tŏrta f (“twisted”). Doublet of torte and tart.

parole.significato: A light, porous form of concretionary limestone (or calcite) deposited from solution, and sometimes quarried for buildi…
parole.testo: From Italian travertino, earlier tivertino, from Latin tīburtīnus (“Tiburtine”).

parole.significato: Calcareous lime deposited by precipitation from a body of water, such as a hot spring.
parole.testo: From Italian tufo, from Latin tōfus or tōphus. Doublet of tuff.

parole.significato: All together. Indicates that the remainder of a group should join in playing after a solo or other passage with a reduc…
parole.testo: From Italian tutti, from Latin totus (“all”).

parole.significato: Synonym of tyro (“a beginner, a novice”).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian tirone, from Latin tīrō (“beginner, novice; young apprentice; (Roman military) recruit”): see further at tyro.

parole.significato: Synonym of umbo.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian umbone, from Latin umbō. Doublet of umbo.

parole.significato: A cloth-covered frame used for protection against rain or sun.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian ombrella (“parasol, sunshade”), from Late Latin umbrella (influenced by umbra (“shadow, shade”)), from Latin umbella, from umbra + -la (diminutive suffix).

parole.significato: Making the noise of waves.
parole.testo: From the Italian undisono, from the Latin undisonus.

parole.significato: Syllable (formerly) used in solfège to represent the first note of a major scale.
parole.testo: From Middle English ut (“first degree or note of Guido of Arezzo's hexachordal scales”), Italian ut in the solmization of Guido of Arezzo, from the opening word Latin ut (“how”) in the lyrics of the scale-ascending hymn Ut queant laxis by Benedictine monk Paulus Deacon (8th c. CE).

parole.significato: An erratic, unpredictable occurrence or action.
parole.testo: From Italian vagare (“wander”) and/or its source Latin vagārī (“to wander”), from Latin vagus (“wandering”). Later apparently reinterpreted in English as vague + -ery but without changing the spelling. By surface analysis, Latin vag(us) + -ary.

parole.significato: A strikingly handsome man, particularly one similar in appearance to Rudolph Valentino.
parole.testo: From Italian Valentino, from Latin Valentīnus (“Valentine”), a patronymic from Valēns (Roman cognomen), itself nominalized from vālens (“strong, healthy”) + -īnus (“-ine”). As a noun, named after Italian-American actor Rudolph Valentino (1895–1926). Doublet of Valentine, Valentinus, Valentina, and V

parole.significato: (To be played) with great rapidity.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian veloce.

parole.significato: Revenge.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian vendetta (“revenge”), from Latin vindicta. See vindicate, avenge.

parole.significato: Any of the nineteen points that divide an ordered distribution into twenty parts, each containing one twentieth of the…
parole.testo: From Italian venti (“twenty”), Late Latin vĭnti, from Latin vīgintī.

parole.significato: Long, slender pasta, similar to spaghetti, only thinner.
parole.testo: From Italian vermicelli, plural of vermicello (“little worm”), from verme (“worm”), from Latin vermis + -cello (“diminutive suffix”).

parole.significato: A type of four-wheeled carriage, especially one let for hire
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian vettura, from Latin vectūra (“conveyance”). Doublet of vecture and voiture.

parole.significato: A house, often larger and more expensive than average, in the countryside or on the coast, often used as a retreat.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian villa, from Latin vīlla (“country house”). Doublet of vill and ville.

parole.significato: An expert in virtù or art objects and antiquities; a connoisseur.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian virtuoso, from Late Latin virtuōsus (“virtuous”), from Latin virtus (“excellence”). Doublet of virtuous.

parole.significato: A distant view or prospect, especially one seen through some opening, avenue or passage.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian vista (“view, sight”), from visto, past participle of vedere (“to see”), from Latin vidēre (“to see”). Compare vision, video, visa.

parole.significato: At a brisk, lively tempo.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian vivace (“brisk, lively”), from Latin vīvāx (“lively, vigorous, energetic”), from vīvō (“live, be alive”).

parole.significato: A vent or fissure on the surface of a planet (usually in a mountainous form) with a magma chamber attached to the mantl…
parole.testo: From Italian vulcano, from Vulcano (“a small volcanic island in the Tyrrhenian Sea”), from Latin Vulcānus (“Vulcan, the Roman god of fire and metalworking”). Doublet of bolcane and Vulcan.

parole.significato: A custard-like dessert made with egg yolks, sugar and Marsala wine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian zabaglione, zabaione, possibly from Latin sabaia (“Illyrian barley beer”) (from an Illyrian word probably from Proto-Indo-European *sab- (“taste”)) + -one (augmentative suffix).

parole.significato: Cobalt oxide obtained by roasting cobalt ore, used as a blue pigment.
parole.testo: From Italian zaffera, from Latin sapphirus (“sapphire”). Doublet of sapphire.

parole.significato: Synonym of socle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian zocco, from Latin soccus. Doublet of sock.
